The graph above shows $y=k{(\frac{1}{3})}^{x}+c.$ Find the value of $k-c.$
question.worked_solution:
The horizontal asymptote of the curve $y=k{(\frac{1}{3})}^{x}+c$ is $y=c.$ In the graph above, the horizontal asymptote is $y=-4.$ Hence, $c=-4.$

We can solve for $k$ by finding a point on the graph and substituting for $x$ and $y.$ The labeled point on the graph is $(0,-2),$ so we substitute $x=0$ and $y=-2$ into the function and solve for $k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}k{(\frac{1}{3})}^{x}+c & =y \\ k{(\frac{1}{3})}^{x}-4 & =y \\ k{(\frac{1}{3})}^{0}-4 & =-2 \\ k-4 & =-2 \\ k & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
k-c=2-(-4)=6.
$$

The equation of the curve is $y=2{(\frac{1}{3})}^{x}-4.$

We can solve for $k$ by finding a point on the graph and substituting for $x$ and $y.$ The labeled point on the graph is $(0,2),$ so we substitute $x=0$ and $y=2$ into the function and solve for $k:$

$$

$$

Therefore, 

$$
k-c=\frac{2}{3}-\frac{4}{3}=-\frac{2}{3}.
$$

The equation of the curve is $y=\frac{2}{3}{(\frac{1}{4})}^{x}+\frac{4}{3}.$

question.knowledge_point: Calculating the Vertical Asymptotes of a Rational Function
question.worked_solution:
To find the vertical asymptotes of a rational function, we factor the numerator and denominator and cancel any common factors. Then, we set the denominator equal to zero and solve for $x.$

There are no common factors in the numerator and denominator, so we set the denominator equal to zero and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+3)(x+1)(x-1) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

This gives the three solutions $x=-3,$ $x=-1$ and $x=1.$ Therefore, the equations of the vertical asymptotes are  $x=-3,\,$ $x=-1$ and $x=1.$

question.knowledge_point: Calculating Vertical Asymptotes When the Denominator Has Complex Roots
question.worked_solution:
To find the vertical asymptotes of a rational function, we factor the numerator and denominator and cancel any common factors. Then, we set the denominator equal to zero and solve for $x:$

Factoring the numerator and denominator, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{{x}^{2}-9}{{x}^{3}-2{x}^{2}+6x-12} \\  & =\frac{(x+3)(x-3)}{{x}^{2}(x-2)+6(x-2)} \\  & =\frac{(x+3)(x-3)}{({x}^{2}+6)(x-2)}\end{aligned}
$$

There are no common factors in the numerator and denominator, so we set the denominator equal to zero. This gives

$$
({x}^{2}+6)(x-2)=0.
$$

We now solve the above equation using the zero product property:

- Solving $x-2=0$ gives the solution $x=2.$

- The equation ${x}^{2}+6=0$ has no real solutions.

Therefore, the only vertical asymptote is $x=2.$

question.knowledge_point: Calculating Vertical Asymptotes With Common Factors When the Denominator Has Complex Roots
question.worked_solution:
To find the vertical asymptotes of a rational function, we factor the numerator and denominator and cancel any common factors. Then, we set the denominator equal to zero and solve for $x.$

Factoring the numerator and denominator and canceling any common factors, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{{x}^{2}-1}{{x}^{4}-1} \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}-1}{({x}^{2}-1)({x}^{2}+1)} \\  & =\frac{(x-1)(x+1)}{(x-1)(x+1)({x}^{2}+1)} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{(x-1)(x+1)}}{\cancel{(x-1)(x+1)}({x}^{2}+1)} \\  & =\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we set the denominator equal to zero:

$$
{x}^{2}+1=0
$$

This equation does not have any real solutions. Therefore, $f(x)$ has no vertical asymptotes.

question.knowledge_point: Calculating Vertical Asymptotes With Common Factors When the Denominator Has Complex Roots
question.worked_solution:
To find the vertical asymptotes of a rational function, we factor the numerator and denominator and cancel any common factors. Then, we set the denominator equal to zero and solve for $x.$

Factoring the numerator and denominator and canceling any common factors, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{2{x}^{2}-6}{{x}^{4}-9} \\  & =\frac{2({x}^{2}-3)}{({x}^{2}-3)({x}^{2}+3)} \\  & =\frac{2\cancel{({x}^{2}-3)}}{\cancel{({x}^{2}-3)}({x}^{2}+3)} \\  & =\frac{2}{{x}^{2}+3}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we set the denominator equal to zero:

$$
{x}^{2}+3=0
$$

This equation does not have any real solutions. Therefore, $f(x)$ has no vertical asymptotes.

question.knowledge_point: Calculating the Slope of a Tangent Line of a Curve With Fractional Powers at a Given Point
question.problem: What is the slope of the tangent to the curve $y=x-\sqrt[3]{x}$ at the point $(8,6)?$
question.worked_solution:
This time, we'll use $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ notation. First, we compute the derivative, which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x-{x}^{1/3}) \\  & =1-\frac{1}{3}\cdot {x}^{-2/3} \\  & =1-\frac{1}{3\sqrt[3]{{x}^{2}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $x=8$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=8} & =1-\frac{1}{3\sqrt[3]{{8}^{2}}} \\  & =1-\frac{1}{12} \\  & =\frac{11}{12}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent to the curve is $\frac{11}{12}.$

question.knowledge_point: Calculating the Slope of a Tangent Line of a Curve With Fractional Powers at a Given Point
question.problem: What is the slope of the tangent to the curve $y={x}^{2}-3x+6\sqrt{x}$ at the point $(4,16)?$
question.worked_solution:
This time, we'll use $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}$ notation. First, we compute the derivative, which gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}-3x+6\sqrt{x}) \\  & =2\cdot x-3+\frac{1}{2}\cdot 6{x}^{-1/2} \\  & =2x-3+3{x}^{-1/2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at $x=4$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=4} & =2(4)-3+3(4{)}^{-1/2} \\  & =8-3+\frac{3}{2} \\  & =\frac{13}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent to the curve is $\frac{13}{2}.$

question.knowledge_point: Finding a Point on a Curve With a Certain Slope
question.problem: Find the $x$-coordinates of the points on the curve $y=-2{x}^{3}+6{x}^{2}+20x-1$ whose tangent has a slope of $2.$
question.worked_solution:
Let $f(x)=-2{x}^{3}+6{x}^{2}+20x-1.$ The slope of the tangent at the point $x$ is equal to ${f}^{′}(x).$ Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(-2{x}^{3}+6{x}^{2}+20x-1) \\  & =-2\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{3})+6\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2})+20\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x)-\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(1) \\  & =-2\cdot 3{x}^{2}+6\cdot 2x+20\cdot 1-0 \\  & =-6{x}^{2}+12x+20.\end{aligned}
$$

We now set ${f}^{′}(x)=2$ and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}-6{x}^{2}+12x+20 & =2 \\ -6{x}^{2}+12x+18 & =0 \\ -6({x}^{2}-2x-3) & =0 \\ -6(x+1)(x-3) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent is equal to $2$ at the points where $x=-1,3.$

question.knowledge_point: Finding a Point on a Curve With a Certain Slope
question.problem: Find the $x$-coordinate of the point on the curve $y={x}^{2}-3x+10$ whose tangent has a slope of $-1.$
question.worked_solution:
Let $f(x)={x}^{2}-3x+10.$ The slope of the tangent at the point $x$ is equal to ${f}^{′}(x).$ Computing the derivative, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}-3x+10) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2})-3\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(x)+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(10) \\  & =2x-3\cdot 1+0 \\  & =2x-3.\end{aligned}
$$

We now set ${f}^{′}(x)=-1$ and solve for $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2x-3 & =-1 \\ 2x & =-1+3 \\ 2x & =2 \\ x & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent is equal to $-1$ at the point where $x=1.$
